Monopolistic Supply

The \(2 \times 2\) Model

Assume the following (see Li, 2019, p. 146):

  1. The economy contains two commodities and two consumers. Commodity 2 is the numeraire commodity, so the price vector is

    \[ \mathbf p=(p_1,1)^\top \]

  2. Consumer 1 is endowed with \(s_1>0\) units of commodity 1, while consumer 2 is endowed with \(s_2>0\) units of commodity 2. The endowment matrix is

\[ \mathbf S= \begin{bmatrix} s_1&0\\ 0&s_2 \end{bmatrix} \]

  1. The two consumers have the same reduced-form CES utility function

    \[ u(x_1,x_2) = (x_1^{-1}+x_2^{-1})^{-1} \]

  2. In the competitive benchmark, both consumers supply their full endowments. In the monopoly case, consumer 1 may choose to supply only \(q\) units of commodity 1, where \(0<q\leq s_1\), while the remaining \(s_1-q\) units are left idle. The production process and the consumption of final products are omitted in this simplified model. Accordingly, the CES utility function is a reduced-form representation of the utility generated through the omitted production and final-product consumption process, while the two commodities themselves represent production factors. Consumer 2 continues to supply its full endowment.

For the above utility function, the demand matrix can be written as

\[ \mathbf D(\mathbf p,\mathbf u) = \begin{bmatrix} u_1\left(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{p_1}}\right) & u_2\left(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{p_1}}\right) \\ u_1(1+\sqrt{p_1}) & u_2(1+\sqrt{p_1}) \end{bmatrix} \]

Analytical Solution

Under full endowment supply, solving the equality-form wide-sense structural equilibrium model gives

\[ \mathbf p^* = \left( \left(\frac{s_2}{s_1}\right)^2, 1 \right)^\top \]

and

\[ u_1^* = \frac{s_1s_2^2}{(s_1+s_2)^2}, \qquad u_2^* = \frac{s_2s_1^2}{(s_1+s_2)^2} \]

For fixed \(s_2\), consumer 1’s equilibrium utility satisfies

\[ \frac{d u_1^*}{d s_1} = \frac{s_2^2(s_2-s_1)}{(s_1+s_2)^3} \]

Hence \(u_1^*\) increases with \(s_1\) when \(s_1<s_2\), decreases with \(s_1\) when \(s_1>s_2\), and reaches its maximum at \(s_1=s_2\).

For any given supply level \(q\) chosen by consumer 1, where \(0<q\leq s_1\), the resulting competitive equilibrium is obtained by replacing \(s_1\) with \(q\). Thus,

\[ p_1(q) = \left(\frac{s_2}{q}\right)^2 \]

and consumer 1’s equilibrium utility is

\[ u_1(q) = \frac{q s_2^2}{(q+s_2)^2} \]

The monopoly supply problem is therefore

\[ \max_{0<q\leq s_1}u_1(q) \]

Since

\[ \frac{d u_1}{dq} = \frac{s_2^2(s_2-q)}{(q+s_2)^3} \]

the optimal supply is

\[ q^* = \min\{s_1,s_2\} \]

In particular, if \(s_1>s_2\),

\[ q^*=s_2<s_1 \]

so consumer 1 increases its equilibrium utility by withholding part of its endowment from the market.

For example, let

\[ s_1=200, \qquad s_2=100 \]

Under full supply, the competitive equilibrium is

\[ \mathbf p^*=(0.25,1)^\top \]

with

\[ u_1^*=22.2222, \qquad u_2^*=44.4444 \]

The monopoly solution is

\[ q^*=100 \]

which gives

\[ \mathbf p^*=(1,1)^\top \]

and

\[ u_1^*=u_2^*=25 \]

Consumer 1 therefore raises its equilibrium utility from approximately \(22.2222\) to \(25\) by reducing its supply from \(200\) to \(100\).

Numerical Solution

The numerical solution treats the monopoly problem as a hierarchical equilibrium problem. For each candidate supply \(q\), the inner problem constructs the corresponding pure-exchange economy and solves its competitive equilibrium with GEMB. The resulting equilibrium utility of consumer 1 is then returned to the outer optimization problem. The numerical procedure can be summarized as

\[ q \longrightarrow \text{competitive equilibrium} \longrightarrow \mathbf p^*(q),\mathbf u^*(q) \longrightarrow u_1^*(q) \longrightarrow \max_q u_1^*(q) \]

With \(s_1=200\) and \(s_2=100\), the numerical solution gives

\[ q^*\approx100, \qquad \mathbf p^*\approx(1,1)^\top \]

and

\[ u_1^*\approx25, \qquad u_2^*\approx25 \]

which agrees with the analytical solution.

References

Li, W. (2019) General equilibrium and structural dynamics: Perspectives of new structural economics. Beijing: Economic Science Press.
